claim.pdf_says: 14.9.40.3   Syntax rules   (printed bold, the same heading style/level as 14.9.40.1 General, 14.9.40.2 General formats and 14.9.41.4 General rules)
claim.why_it_matters: A fourth-level clause is transcribed at markdown level 2, the same level as its own parent '## 14.9.40 SORT statement', so in the generated outline 14.9.40.3 becomes a sibling of 14.9.40 rather than a child of it. Its own siblings are inconsistent: 14.9.40.1 and 14.9.40.2 are '###', and every corresponding heading in the neighbouring START clause (14.9.41.1 through 14.9.41.4) is '###'. Section-navigation and any anchor/TOC generation built on heading depth mis-nest this clause.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED. Nothing is missing and nothing is altered; the claim is a markdown-internal style quibble with no counterpart in the PDF. (1) The heading is PRESENT and VERBATIM CORRECT. PDF p.776 (printed folio 746) prints '14.9.40.3 Syntax rules'; specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 31497 reads '## 14.9.40.3 Syntax rules' preceded by its explicit anchor '' at line 31496. Same number, same title, same position (immediately after the Format 2 (table) diagram, immediately before 'ALL FORMATS' / rules 1)-6)). The kind label 'missing-heading' is a misnomer: no heading is missing. (2) The PDF carries NO level information to contradict. I rendered p.775 and p.776 and looked at the glyphs. On p.775 '14.9.40 SORT statement', '14.9.40.1 General' and '14.9.40.2 General formats' are all set in the SAME bold face at the SAME point size; on p.776 '14.9.40.3 Syntax rules' is set identically. The ISO typography does not visually distinguish a third-level from a fourth-level clause here, so the claim's premise -- that the PDF asserts a level the markdown got wrong -- is false. Markdown heading depth in this transcription is an editorial convention inferred from the dotted section number, not a fact read off the page. The number '14.9.40.3' is itself present in the heading text and states the nesting unambiguously. (3) The claim MISQUOTES its own comparison set and misstates the sibling pattern. It cites '14.9.41.4 General rules' (a different clause, in START) as the style anchor while omitting the actual sibling, 14.9.40.4 General rules, which is at line 31573 and is ALSO '##'. The real pattern is .1/.2 = '###' and .3/.4 = '##' -- so 14.9.40.3 is not an outlier among its siblings; it matches 14.9.40.4. The identical split appears in the immediately preceding clause: 14.9.39.1/.2 are '###' (lines 30741, 30763) while 14.9.39.3/.4 are '##' (lines 30949, 31160). (4) It is a document-wide transcription convention, not a page-776 discrepancy. Across specs/ISO_COBOL.md, 162 four-part headings are '##' and 620 are '###'. Ledgering this as a per-page structural finding on p.776 would require ledgering 161 identical findings elsewhere; it is a global style question about the transcription, not a divergence from the canonical PDF on this page. (5) The stated harm does not obtain. The document's TOC is a TRANSCRIPTION of the PDF's own printed table of contents with explicit page links (e.g. line 867: '[14.9.40 SORT statement](#section-14-9-40) ... [745](#page-745)'), not a depth-generated outline. Navigation targets are explicit '' anchors, which are wholly independent of '#' count. So neither anchor resolution nor TOC generation is affected. Per the reconciliation rules -- reject when the text is present, when the difference is only formatting, and when meaning is unchanged -- all three grounds apply. No normative content, syntax rule, general rule, or general format is affected.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy. The heading '14.9.40.3 Syntax rules' is transcribed completely and correctly at the correct position, with its explicit anchor. The only difference is the markdown '#' count, which the PDF does not specify -- ISO sets 14.9.40, 14.9.40.1, 14.9.40.2 and 14.9.40.3 in one identical bold face at one identical size. If tracked at all, this belongs as a single document-wide style item, not a page finding: 162 of the 782 four-part-numbered headings in specs/ISO_COBOL.md use '##' where 620 use '###' (14.9.40.3 and 14.9.40.4 are '##' while 14.9.40.1 and 14.9.40.2 are '###'; 14.9.39 splits the same way). No content, anchor, or TOC behaviour is impacted, since the TOC is transcribed with explicit page/section links rather than generated from heading depth.
